rows: Send the worker's answer without what the page does not read. The worker ran the whole program on the interpreter and sent back every probe sample with its environment, closures and all, and a trace, about 5 MB of terms; the picture waited for it. Two cuts (no function-holding values in the samples' environments, no trace), then no sharing between answers. Later the answer went without a stream the page dropped on arrival, and its first-order values as data (590 KB to 198 KB).

A step's picture 4.17 to 6.52 s on build 1, 1.85 to 2.38 s on build 2, 1.33 to 1.71 s on build 3 (^report(46)). The answer 590 KB to 198 KB on build 20; the worker's encode 72 to 107 ms to 21 to 29, the page's decode 24 to 31 ms to 7 to 8. 2.84 s to 4.81 s off a step.
The picture no longer waits for the worker. Its answer still comes 1.5 to 2.4 s after a step, and costs the page 7 to 10 ms to decode.

Compile the slide's whole run to JavaScript, each livelit's model a parameter. hazel-jit compiles the slide's elaborated program once into a JavaScript function whose parameters are the livelits' models. A slider's event calls it with the new model, and every livelit draws from its answers at the page's next redraw, before the worker has answered.

A step's picture 1.33 to 1.71 s on build 3, 208 to 236 ms on build 5 (steps 2 to 4; ^report(49)). In Node, a slider's step 684 ms on the interpreter, 2.3 to 2.5 ms compiled (^report(45)). 1.09 s to 1.50 s off a step.
It is why a step shows in about 20 ms: the run answers in 2 to 3 ms (5 to 12 for a step's first event).
+1,307 / −12 in 6; and +506 in hazel-jit's own modules

Draw first; make the edit after the paint. When the compiled run has answered a slider's event, the page draws at once and writes the new model into the program (the edit: update, statics, syntax and the whole view) only after the browser has painted, at the next animation frame.
A step's picture 152 to 195 ms on build 11, 19 to 24 ms on build 12 (steps 2 to 4; ^report(51)). 133 ms to 171 ms off a step.
The edit still runs after the paint: 75 to 90 ms, the largest single piece of a step's work left. ^ticket(721) takes on most of it.
+35 / −1 in 1; and +5 in hazel-jit's own modules
Compile each livelit's view. A livelit's view, a Hazel function from its model to HTML, compiled by hazel-jit and drawn straight from its JavaScript, not stepped through by the interpreter.

The Witch's picture view in the app, in Firefox: 87 ms a render on the interpreter, 3.0 ms compiled (^report(46)). A Polygons render in Node, 14.1 ms to 0.38 (^report(45)). 84 ms off each render of the picture.
In a drag, a livelit drawn from JS takes about 1 ms, against 4.6 ms with nothing compiled (builds 30 to 39).
+606 / −333 in 4; and +4,328 in hazel-jit's own modules

A drag redraws only what changed. Four cuts to a drag's frame: its input goes to the page as a request to draw again, not to the editor as an edit (cut A); only the livelits whose answers changed are drawn again (cut B); the projectors' data and finished views are kept while nothing they read changed (cut C); and each editor's decorations and probes' views are kept across frames.

A 3-second drag of the Witch's neck slider: 9.8 fps on build 5, 22.5 on build 6 (cut A), 26.4 on build 7, 48.4 on build 8, 57.6 on build 12: a frame from 102 ms to 17.4 (^report(50) and ^report(51)). 80 ms to 85 ms off each frame of a drag.
A drag runs at 55 to 58 fps, its view 5 to 7 ms a frame.

Keep the livelits a change did not touch. A livelit's finished view is kept, keyed on what it reads (its own statics record, its own samples and those it looked up, compared by value) rather than on the whole statics map and the whole run. So after an edit only the edited livelit is drawn again, and after the worker's answer only those whose samples changed. The same for its shape, its applied definition and its wrapper, for the probes and the sidebar's problem list.

The page's work after a step 0.43 to 0.60 s on build 13, 0.24 to 0.30 s on build 15 (machines alike; ^report(51)). After an answer 4 projectors drawn, not 56 (build 19); at the answer the projectors' views 16 to 41 ms on build 26, 11 to 16 on build 31; after an edit the probes' views 4 to 13 ms on build 35, 1 to 3 on build 37. 190 ms to 400 ms off a step.
Of the 53 livelits, 51 keep their views at each answer and after each edit.

Build the outline on its own, and only what changed. The sidebar's outline of the slide's program was built inside the page's view, after every edit and every message from the worker. It is now built on its own after the paint; it redraws the page only when it changed; it keys the run's test results by each test's status; and its search for rows that open no cell walks only the top-level tiles an edit changed.

The views after each worker message 88 to 130 ms on build 12, 45 to 63 on build 13 (two messages a step); after an answer the outline's 59 to 82 ms gone (build 19); the outline after an edit 42 to 53 ms on build 21, 18 on build 36; its mark in the view 5 to 14 ms on build 40, 0 on build 41. 128 ms to 201 ms off a step.
The outline after an edit, 18 to 42 ms, runs as a task of its own.

Compile the run once; compare only what changed. The slide's run was compiled again after every step. Now it is kept while only models change: the new program is compared with the compiled one, models left out, and the comparison erases only the nodes a step changed.
126 to 141 ms of compiling after each step on build 8; 29 to 51 ms of comparing on build 9; 1 ms on build 17 (^report(50) and ^report(51)). 125 ms to 140 ms off a step.
The comparison takes about 1 ms a step; the run is kept at every step.
+172 / −122 in 3; and +492 in hazel-jit's own modules

Save without a redraw, printing only what changed. The autosave went through the page's update, so each save was followed by a calculate, a whole view and an outline. It now writes the model directly, and prints again only the top-level pieces a step changed.
About 60 ms gone after each autosave (build 16); the autosave itself 38 to 67 ms on build 21, 21 to 31 on build 23. 77 ms to 96 ms off a step.
The autosave takes 16 to 31 ms, about a second after a step.

Draw the picture's probe row without rewriting its value. The probe on the picture abbreviated its value by rewriting all of it first, and checked whether each sample was a value by running the evaluator's step rules over the whole value. It now abbreviates in one pass, and answers plain data by its shape.
The probe row after each answer 44 to 91 ms on build 13, 8 to 21 on build 14; 15 to 35 ms on build 24, 3 to 6 on build 26. 38 ms to 85 ms off each answer.
The probe row takes 3 to 6 ms at each answer.

section: Redoing it by hand, in small increments
rows: The Firefox check that drives the Witch slide and times each step and drag (scripts/jit_slides.py, .github/workflows/jit.yml), the page's timeline of marks (Util.BenchMarks) and the worker's answer weighed by part (AnswerParts). It changes nothing a user sees; with it, each later increment is measured the way this report's builds were.
672 in scripts and CI; 91 and 531 in the two modules
Ingredient A1. The worker and its messages only; it helps dev as much as the livelits branch.
The ingredients that need no hazel-jit: the outline on its own (B2), the autosave without a redraw (B4), the probe row (B5). Each its own small PR.
the outline and autosave: the livelits branch; the probe row: dev
Ingredient B1: a livelit's view, shape and applied definition keyed on what it reads. Several small PRs, one cache each, each with a test that the cache gives the same view.

hazel-jit itself: 2,975 lines in four modules (the values' bridge, the compiler, the DOM, the run), with 2,063 lines of tests that each compiled program agrees with the interpreter. The largest piece, and the one that most needs review by hand; it can land a module at a time.
Ingredient A4: livelit views drawn from compiled JS.
